title: The frequency by regularity interaction
trap: Being irregular slows every word down by about the same amount.
text: The cost of being irregular depends on frequency. High-frequency exception words are named about as fast as high-frequency regular words. Low-frequency exception words are much slower than low-frequency regular words. So the frequency effect is much larger for exception words. The dual-route view says the fast lexical process protects frequent words from decoding. The triangle model says frequent words are learned so well that inconsistency with other words matters less.

title: Why a double dissociation is stronger than one deficit
trap: If one patient group is worse at pseudowords, pseudoword reading must use its own separate process.
text: One group doing worse on one task could mean that task is simply harder. A double dissociation needs a second group with the reverse pattern. Phonological dyslexia hurts pseudowords and spares exception words. Surface dyslexia hurts exception words and spares pseudowords. Because the pattern reverses, one task cannot just be harder for everyone, so the two tasks rely on separable processes.

title: The triangle model is not the dual-route model renamed
trap: The triangle model's OP and SP pathways are just the DRC's two routes with new names.
text: The DRC's routes are modular. They use different processing assumptions and only meet at the phoneme output. The DRC lexicon is also independent of meaning. In the triangle model, semantics is directly involved, and the OP and SP mappings share the same probabilistic learning algorithm. The pathways interact during learning, so the OP pathway develops differently alongside semantics. That is why the triangle model expects double dissociations never to be entirely clean.

title: Poor nonword reading in the first PDP model
trap: The early PDP model's poor nonword reading means one associative mechanism cannot read nonwords.
text: A failed simulation can mean the theory is wrong or that the model was badly made. Seidenberg and McClelland used Wickelfeatures, which fail to capture which words sound similar. Generalization depends on similarity, so nonwords suffered most. Plaut and colleagues (1996) improved the phonological representations and nonword reading got better. So the failure was at least partly in the implementation, not the single-route idea.

title: Runned is a sign of learning
trap: When a child switches from ran to runned, the child has forgotten the irregular form and is going backward.
text: U-shaped learning means children get worse before they get better. Runned is a regularization, which is the regular pattern applied to an irregular verb. In the Words and Rules account, it appears because the child has just learned the add -ed rule and applies it to every verb. In Rumelhart and McClelland's model, it appears because more regular verbs entered the input and the network reorganized. Either way, runned comes from new learning, and ran returns later.

title: A better fit is not always a better model
trap: The DRC's excellent fit to the Woollams patients means it explains them better than the triangle model.
text: Coltheart and colleagues (2009) generated 40,000 model patients and picked the best match for each real patient. The fit was excellent, but it came after seeing the data. A model with that much freedom can match almost any pattern. The triangle model instead predicted the association between semantics and exception reading in advance. So goodness of fit means less when it comes from great flexibility.

title: What Li and Gleitman actually found
trap: Outdoors, English speakers switched to absolute coding like Tzeltal speakers.
text: With the blinds down, English speakers overwhelmingly used relative position. With the blinds up or outdoors, their relative preference was only less pronounced. With the blinds up or outdoors, people split, with some giving all relative answers and others all absolute answers. So the group as a whole did not switch to absolute. Levinson and colleagues (2002) then added memory load and made the rotation less obvious, and the relative bias remained. So the environment matters when the task is easy, but the relative bias holds when memory matters.

title: Deafness, not signing, enhances peripheral attention
trap: Learning sign language enhances attention to the visual periphery.
text: Bavelier and colleagues (2001) included hearing signers to separate signing from deafness. Learning sign shifts motion-perception areas from right to left in both deaf and hearing signers. Enhanced peripheral attention appears only in deaf signers. So signing experience changes laterality, while deafness itself enhances peripheral attention.
